item.title: 🚨 Shadow AI: The AI Your Organisation Doesn’t Know It’s Using
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: “Are our employees using AI?” If your immediate answer is “Not really” or “We don’t think so”, you might want to keep reading. Because here’s the uncomfortable truth: AI adoption is moving much faster than most organisations can govern it. Employees are already using AI to write emails, summarise meetings, analyse spreadsheets, create presentations, write […]
item.content:encoded:
“Are our employees using AI?”

If your immediate answer is “Not really” or “We don’t think so”, you might want to keep reading.

Because here’s the uncomfortable truth:

AI adoption is moving much faster than most organisations can govern it.

Employees are already using AI to write emails, summarise meetings, analyse spreadsheets, create presentations, write code, research customers and generally make their working lives easier.

And why wouldn’t they?

If something takes an hour and AI can get it down to ten minutes, people are going to use it.

The problem isn’t necessarily that employees are doing something wrong.

The problem is that you might not know what they’re doing.

Welcome to the world of Shadow AI.

So… what exactly is Shadow AI?

Let’s keep this simple.

Shadow AI is AI being used without the knowledge, approval or governance of the organisation.

It could be an employee copying a customer email into a public AI chatbot and asking it to write a response.

It could be someone uploading a spreadsheet containing sensitive information and asking AI to analyse it.

It could be a developer using an AI coding assistant that hasn’t been approved.

Or someone in HR asking an online AI service to summarise a document containing employee information.

And here’s the interesting part:

They might not be trying to break any rules.

They might simply be trying to do their job.

They’ve found a tool that saves them time, makes their work easier or helps them solve a problem.

And that’s precisely why Shadow AI is such a difficult governance problem.

The employee isn’t necessarily the problem.

The lack of visibility is.

The uncomfortable truth

For years, we’ve built increasingly sophisticated controls around organisational information.

We ask:

Where is it stored?

Who can access it?

How is it protected?

How long should we keep it?

Then AI came along and changed the game.

Suddenly, an employee doesn’t necessarily need to give an AI system direct access to an information repository.

They can simply copy the information into the AI.

And that changes the governance question.

It is no longer just:

“Who has access to our information?”

It’s becoming:

“Where is our information going, what is being done with it, and who or what is processing it?”

That’s a much bigger question.

So what’s the actual risk?

There are three big ones.

1. Data leakage

This is the obvious one.

Someone takes sensitive information and puts it into an AI service outside the organisation’s controlled environment.

It might be:

  • Customer information
  • Financial data
  • Personal information
  • Intellectual property
  • Commercial plans
  • Internal documents
  • Source code

The employee might think:

“I’ll just paste this in and ask AI to summarise it.”

But suddenly the organisation has some serious questions to answer.

Where did the information go?

Who processed it?

What controls applied?

What happened to the output?

And perhaps most importantly:

Can we prove what happened?

2. Compliance gaps

Organisations have rules.

Regulatory requirements.

Contractual obligations.

Legal responsibilities.

Internal policies.

All of those things exist for a reason.

But here’s the problem:

Your policies don’t automatically follow your data into every AI tool on the internet.

If employees are using unmanaged AI services, there can be a significant gap between:

What your organisation says should happen

and

What is actually happening.

And that gap?

That’s where governance problems start.

3. You simply don’t know

This might actually be the biggest problem.

Which AI tools are people using?

Who is using them?

How often?

Why?

What information are they putting into them?

And are some employees regularly handling sensitive information through unmanaged AI?

If you don’t know the answers, you’re not really governing AI.

You’re guessing.

And guessing isn’t a particularly great governance strategy.

“But we have Microsoft 365 Copilot…”

Great.

That is an important part of your AI strategy.

But it doesn’t mean Shadow AI has disappeared.

Microsoft 365 Copilot is an enterprise AI capability designed to operate within the Microsoft 365 ecosystem and work with your organisation’s identity, permissions and security controls.

But here’s the important question:

What other AI are your employees using alongside Copilot?

Because an organisation can have a perfectly good Microsoft 365 Copilot deployment…

…and still have employees using external AI services every day.

That’s where the Shadow AI conversation gets interesting.

Here’s the Shadow AI paradox

People aren’t using Shadow AI because they hate their organisation.

They’re using it because it works.

Think about it.

You have a difficult email.

AI can help.

You’ve got a huge document.

AI can summarise it.

You’ve got a spreadsheet.

AI can analyse it.

You’ve got a presentation to create.

AI can help.

You’ve got some code that isn’t behaving.

AI might know why.

And if something takes an hour manually but five minutes with AI…

Which option do you think people are going to choose?

Exactly.

So here’s one of the most important things organisations need to understand:

You cannot govern AI effectively by pretending people won’t use it.

The technology is already here.

The challenge is creating an environment where people can use it safely and responsibly.

Should we just block everything?

Ah, the classic IT response. We’ve all been there right?

“Block it.”

Sometimes that’s absolutely the right answer.

But making “block AI” your entire strategy probably isn’t going to end well.

Because if employees are getting genuine value from AI, they’ll keep looking for ways to use it.

Block one application?

Another appears.

Don’t provide an approved alternative?

People find their own.

And suddenly you’ve pushed the behaviour further underground.

So perhaps the better question isn’t:

“How do we stop people using AI?”

It’s:

“How do we make it safe for people to use AI?”

That means providing trusted alternatives, protecting sensitive information, establishing clear guidance and applying sensible controls.

The first step isn’t blocking. It’s visibility.

Before you reach for the block button, ask a much more useful question:

“What AI are our employees actually using?”

That’s where things get interesting.

You want to understand:

Which tools are being used?

Who is using them?

How often?

Why?

What information could be involved?

Which applications represent the greatest risk?

Once you have those answers, Shadow AI stops being an abstract concern.

It becomes something you can actually measure, understand and manage.

From “we think” to “we know”

Imagine asking your organisation:

“Are employees using AI tools outside Microsoft 365?”

Someone might respond:

“Probably not very much.”

Hmm.

Now imagine being able to say:

“We’ve identified 1,200 employees interacting with external AI applications over the last 90 days.”

Different conversation, isn’t it?

Now you can ask:

Which applications?

Which departments?

Which users?

Which applications are approved?

Which aren’t?

Where is sensitive information involved?

Where do we need controls?

This is why discovery is the turning point.

It takes you from:

Assumption → Evidence

And that’s where real governance begins.

Control the apps. Control the data.

Once you understand what’s happening, you’ve got something much more useful than a list of scary headlines.

You’ve got information you can act on.

I think about Shadow AI governance around two fundamental questions.

1. Which AI applications are we comfortable with?

Assess them against things like:

  • Security
  • Privacy
  • Data handling
  • Compliance
  • Vendor risk
  • Business need
  • Regulatory requirements
  • Organisational policy

Then classify them.

Approved.

Restricted.

Monitored.

Blocked.

Because not every AI application presents the same risk.

2. What information can people put into them?

This might actually be the more important question.

Imagine two prompts.

“Rewrite this generic paragraph.”

Pretty harmless.

Now:

“Summarise this document containing confidential customer information.”

Same AI tool.

Very different risk.

That’s why AI governance and information governance are so closely connected.

Classification.

Sensitivity labels.

DLP.

Access controls.

Retention.

Monitoring.

Audit.

All suddenly become part of the AI conversation.

The question changes from:

“Can I use this AI tool?”

to:

“What am I allowed to put into this AI tool?”

And that is a much more mature governance conversation.

The biggest Shadow AI mistake

It’s tempting to think the answer is simply:

Block.

But blocking everything isn’t governance.

It’s a reaction.

A better model is:

Discover → Assess → Govern → Protect → Monitor

First, understand what is happening.

Then assess the risk.

Decide what controls are appropriate.

Protect the information that matters.

And keep monitoring.

Because AI isn’t standing still.

New applications will appear.

Existing applications will gain new capabilities.

Employees will discover new ways of using them.

And increasingly, AI agents will be able to interact with business systems and information.

The Shadow AI challenge isn’t going away.

It’s probably going to get more interesting.

This isn’t just an IT problem

Here’s another thing worth remembering.

Shadow AI touches almost everyone.

IT

Which applications are being used?

Security

What risks do they introduce?

Information Governance

What information is being processed?

Compliance

Are our obligations being met?

HR

What are employees permitted to do?

Legal

What are our obligations around data and intellectual property?

Business Leadership

How do we capture the productivity benefits without taking unnecessary risks?

This isn’t something you can simply throw over the wall to the IT department.

AI governance needs a joined-up approach.

And then there’s Copilot…

This is where things get particularly interesting for Microsoft 365 organisations.

Microsoft 365 Copilot provides an enterprise AI capability within the Microsoft ecosystem.

But there’s an important point:

Copilot can work with the information the user already has access to.

So if your Microsoft 365 environment contains years of overshared documents, messy permissions and information that has accumulated without proper governance…

Copilot doesn’t magically clean that up.

In fact, AI could make those existing issues far more visible and potentially more consequential.

Which brings us to a rather important question:

Are you ready for AI to help people discover the information they already have access to?

Where does Purview fit?

This is where Microsoft Purview becomes particularly interesting.

Purview can form an important part of the wider information governance strategy, helping organisations understand, protect and govern their information.

But I wouldn’t think of Purview simply as another security product.

Think of it as part of your organisation’s information control layer.

Ask:

Where is our sensitive information?

How is it classified?

Who can access it?

How is it being shared?

What policies apply?

What needs to be retained?

What needs to be deleted?

What happens when we need to investigate something?

And increasingly:

“How should this information be governed when AI gets involved?”

Because AI governance without information governance is going to be difficult.

You can’t safely govern AI if you don’t understand the information AI is interacting with.

So what should organisations actually do?

Don’t panic.

You don’t need to solve every AI governance problem tomorrow.

Start somewhere sensible.

01 – Get visibility

Find out which AI applications are being used.

Don’t guess.

Find the evidence.

02 – Find your highest-risk scenarios

Focus on sensitive information, regulated data and intellectual property.

03 – Give people safe alternatives

If employees are using AI because it makes them more productive, give them an approved way to achieve the same outcome.

04 – Protect the data

Use the controls already available to you – information protection, DLP, classification and appropriate access controls.

05 – Give people clear guidance

Don’t just tell employees:

“You can’t do this.”

Tell them:

“Here’s what you can do.”

06 – Keep watching

AI governance isn’t a project with a completion date.

The landscape will keep moving.

The goal isn’t to stop AI

This is probably the biggest message I’d take away from the whole Shadow AI conversation.

The goal isn’t to stop employees using AI.

It isn’t to block every application.

And it certainly isn’t to write a 50-page AI policy that nobody reads.

The goal is much simpler:

Make AI useful, safe and governable.

Understand what’s happening.

Protect the information that matters.

Provide trusted alternatives.

And put sensible controls around the technology.

That’s the sweet spot.

And then things get really interesting…

We’re still relatively early in the AI journey.

Today’s Shadow AI might be an employee copying text into a chatbot.

Tomorrow?

It could be an AI agent connecting to multiple business systems, accessing information, making decisions and taking actions on someone’s behalf.

Suddenly, the questions become very different.

Not just:

“What information did the employee give the AI?”

But:

“What information can the agent access?”

“What can it do?”

“Who authorised it?”

“What decisions did it make?”

“What actions did it take?”

And perhaps the most important question of all:

“Can we prove what happened?”

You can’t govern what you can’t see

And perhaps that’s what Shadow AI really comes down to.

It isn’t fundamentally an AI problem.

It’s a visibility, information and governance problem that AI has brought into the spotlight.

The organisations that get this right won’t necessarily be the ones with the biggest list of blocked applications.

They’ll be the ones that understand:

What AI is being used.

Who is using it.

Why they’re using it.

What information is involved.

What risks exist.

And what controls are appropriate.

Because let’s face it…

Your employees are probably already using AI.

The real question is:

Do you know how?

And are you ready to govern what happens next?

You can’t govern what you can’t see.

And as AI becomes an increasingly important part of everyday work, seeing, understanding and governing AI activity could become one of the defining challenges of modern Microsoft 365 governance.

The Jim Talks takeaway

Don’t start your AI governance journey by asking, “What should we block?”

Start by asking, “What is actually happening?”

Visibility first. Governance second. Control follows.

item.title: Taking inspiration from… Saw 5?
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Yes, you read that right. Again, hear me out. I am a big believer in shared interests and finding things we can enjoy with others. When the chance came to watch a horror film with a loved one, I was sure it was something we could enjoy and discuss afterwards. The film came and went. […]
item.content:encoded:
Yes, you read that right. Again, hear me out.

I am a big believer in shared interests and finding things we can enjoy with others. When the chance came to watch a horror film with a loved one, I was sure it was something we could enjoy and discuss afterwards.

The film came and went. However, something quite unexpected happened… I was inspired, and not in a “movie” type of way.

The film follows a group of people trapped in a situation where they must overcome challenges to survive. Then came an incredible revelation: the challenges were never designed for individuals to overcome alone. They were designed for the group to work together, allowing everyone to make it to the end.

Whilst taking some time to reflect on that, I found myself applying that principle to daily life. We all face problems every day, and we all could benefit from each other’s experiences.

The problems I am experiencing today are the problems someone experienced yesterday, and someone else will experience tomorrow.

That is how we can look after each other. Knowledge sharing, reassurance, simply leaning on each other.  

None of us have to solve everything alone. Sometimes the answer we need is sitting with someone who has already faced the same challenge…

And that is the value of helping others: we don’t just solve problems for people; we make sure fewer people have to face them alone.

People are better when we stop seeing each other as obstacles and start seeing each other as support.

Who’d have thought that Saw 5 of all things would have given such a powerful message?

item.title: 🔍 Troubleshooting Microsoft Purview eDiscovery Just Got Easier
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: If you’ve ever spent far too long trying to work out why an eDiscovery case isn’t behaving as expected, a new Microsoft Purview update could make life considerably easier. Microsoft is introducing self-service diagnostics for eDiscovery, designed to help administrators identify and resolve some of the common configuration issues that can prevent eDiscovery from working […]
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever spent far too long trying to work out why an eDiscovery case isn’t behaving as expected, a new Microsoft Purview update could make life considerably easier.

Microsoft is introducing self-service diagnostics for eDiscovery, designed to help administrators identify and resolve some of the common configuration issues that can prevent eDiscovery from working as expected.

So, what’s changing?

The new diagnostic experience will help administrators troubleshoot areas including:

  • Case permissions – identify potential permission-related issues.
  • Security filters – highlight configuration problems that could affect search and discovery.
  • Policy status and configuration – identify potential issues with relevant policies and their configuration.

Rather than having to manually work through multiple settings and configurations, the new experience will highlight potential problems and provide guided recommendations to help resolve them.

Why does this matter?

As I am sure many of us know, eDiscovery can become complicated very quickly.

When a search doesn’t return the expected results, or a user can’t access the information they need, the underlying cause isn’t always immediately obvious. Is it a permissions issue? A security filter? A policy that hasn’t been configured correctly?

Previously, troubleshooting could involve working through multiple areas of the Microsoft Purview environment before finding the problem.

The introduction of self-service diagnostics brings some of that troubleshooting directly into the product.

That means administrators should be able to identify common issues faster, understand what’s causing them and take appropriate corrective action without immediately resorting to lengthy investigations or support cases.

Another step towards a more manageable Purview experience

This is perhaps not the most headline-grabbing Microsoft 365 update, but for the people who actually administer eDiscovery, it’s the type of improvement that can make a significant difference.

Microsoft Purview continues to become increasingly capable — but as functionality grows, configuration and troubleshooting can become increasingly complex.

Anything that helps administrators understand “why isn’t this working?” more quickly is therefore a welcome addition.

And there’s an interesting broader trend here: Microsoft is increasingly building guided diagnostics and recommendations directly into its compliance and governance tooling, helping administrators move from simply identifying problems to understanding how to resolve them.

When is it coming?

Public Preview: October 2026
General Availability: November 2026
Microsoft 365 Roadmap: 565222

The takeaway

eDiscovery is powerful — but power brings complexity.

Self-service diagnostics won’t remove that complexity, but it should make some of the most common troubleshooting scenarios considerably easier to navigate.

For organisations relying heavily on Microsoft Purview for compliance, investigations and eDiscovery, this is a small but useful improvement worth keeping an eye on.

item.title: 🔐 Microsoft Purview DLP Gets Smarter with Automated Alert Management
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Security teams spend valuable time reviewing alerts that often follow predictable patterns. Microsoft is helping reduce that burden with a new Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) capability: rule-based alert tagging and auto-resolution. With this enhancement, organisations can define rules that automatically handle DLP alerts based on business needs: ✅ Automatically resolve low-priority alerts that […]
item.content:encoded:
Security teams spend valuable time reviewing alerts that often follow predictable patterns. Microsoft is helping reduce that burden with a new Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention (DLP) capability: rule-based alert tagging and auto-resolution.

With this enhancement, organisations can define rules that automatically handle DLP alerts based on business needs:

Automatically resolve low-priority alerts that don’t require investigation, helping reduce noise in security queues.

Automatically tag alerts to simplify filtering, routing, and reporting. For example, alerts generated by the Legal department can be categorised as a specific business process.

This new capability can help security and compliance teams focus on the alerts that matter most while improving operational efficiency across the organisation.

Preview: August 2026
General Availability: September 2026
Availability: Worldwide (Standard Multi-Tenant)
Roadmap ID: 568371

A welcome enhancement for organisations looking to streamline DLP operations and reduce alert fatigue.

item.title: 🔐 🔐 Microsoft Purview is finally bringing sensitivity labels to SharePoint data at rest
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: I’m excited to see Microsoft Purview Information Protection introducing the ability to automatically apply a SharePoint document library’s default sensitivity label to existing files (data at rest). Today, default sensitivity labels help ensure that new and modified documents are classified correctly. However, many organisations still have thousands of legacy documents that remain unlabelled or inconsistently […]
item.content:encoded:
I’m excited to see Microsoft Purview Information Protection introducing the ability to automatically apply a SharePoint document library’s default sensitivity label to existing files (data at rest).

Today, default sensitivity labels help ensure that new and modified documents are classified correctly. However, many organisations still have thousands of legacy documents that remain unlabelled or inconsistently classified.

With Microsoft 365 Roadmap ID 559105, Microsoft is closing that gap.

What this means

When enabled, SharePoint will be able to evaluate documents already stored within a library and automatically apply the library’s configured default sensitivity label to files that aren’t already appropriately classified.

This brings the same protection model used for new content to historical content as well.

Why it matters

Improved compliance – Legacy documents can be brought into alignment with organisational data protection policies.

Consistent classification – Reduces situations where files within the same library have different or missing labels.

Reduced administrative overhead – No more large-scale manual relabelling exercises for existing content.

Stronger Zero Trust posture – Helps ensure that sensitive information is consistently identified, classified and protected.

Better governance – Supports requirements where all content within a repository must carry the correct protection label.

Real-world examples

HR libraries where historical employee records automatically receive a Confidential – HR label.

Finance repositories where years of financial reports inherit the correct confidentiality classification.

Legal document stores where legacy contracts become consistently protected without manual intervention.

Migration projects where content moved from file shares or third-party platforms can automatically receive the appropriate sensitivity label after migration.

For organisations investing in Microsoft Purview, this feels like a significant step forward. Sensitivity labels become far more valuable when they can help protect not only future content, but also the vast amount of information that’s already stored across SharePoint.

Sometimes the most impactful security improvements are the ones that quietly solve longstanding operational challenges.

item.title: The answer is… Rik Mayall?
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Crazy headline right? I thought so too. However, just hear me out. I was once asked to do a large presentation on all things Microsoft 365. Scary stuff. In my research on how to cope with the nerves, I came across a video of English comedian Rik Mayall (pan-global phenomenon),  giving a speech at Exeter […]
item.content:encoded:
Crazy headline right? I thought so too. However, just hear me out.

I was once asked to do a large presentation on all things Microsoft 365. Scary stuff. In my research on how to cope with the nerves, I came across a video of English comedian Rik Mayall (pan-global phenomenon),  giving a speech at Exeter University.

Inspiring words I thought, until I heard Rik mention that everyone is equal, and therefore nobody is inherently more valuable than anyone else.

The instant I heard those words, the cloud disappeared. Life changing for me that was. Are we all equal? Yes, we are human beings and everyone has different jobs, different expertise, but nobody is worth more than anyone else. So I asked myself,

Why on earth would I be afraid of standing up and talking in front of other human beings?

And from that moment on, something changed. The presentation went ok, it was early days for me on that front and there is always room for improvement. But the fear of standing up in front of people and talking was gone.

There are so many things I took away from Rik Mayall’s words that day. It’s never been lost on me how valuable other people are, and how we can choose to lift each other. Sometimes we should put a bit more trust in the people around us rather than shying away from something. And most of all, never be afraid to do something awesome because of another human being. The right people will applaud you for it.

I have lost count of the number of people I have spoken to over the years who expressed a desire to avoid something through fear – my response has always been the same, “the answer is Rik Mayall”. That’s a lesson I have always tried to pass on, and I will always be grateful to Rik Mayall (the man, the myth, the legend) for inspiring me to move past something that had previously held me back for more years that I can remember!

If there is one thing I’d love for you to take away from this post, its that once you realise you’re simply talking to other human beings, not judges, not superheroes, not people who matter more than you, the fear starts to lose its grip.

item.title: 🚨 Important Update: Microsoft 365 Cost Management Enhancements for Copilot Credits and Usage-Based Billing
item.dc:creator: JimTalksGovernance
item.description: Microsoft is rolling out a series of updates to Cost Management in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center, designed to improve reliability, predictability, and the overall administrator experience for usage-based AI services such as Cowork and Work IQ APIs. 📅 Rollout begins 22 July 2026 and is expected to complete by the end of July. Key […]
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is rolling out a series of updates to Cost Management in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center, designed to improve reliability, predictability, and the overall administrator experience for usage-based AI services such as Cowork and Work IQ APIs.

Rollout begins 22 July 2026 and is expected to complete by the end of July.

Key improvements

More reliable spending alerts

  • Fixes an issue where spending alert thresholds could fail to save or unexpectedly reset.
  • Existing spending alert values will be cleared as part of the update.
  • Administrators will need to recreate any spending alerts they wish to retain.
  • Existing spending limits and policy settings remain unaffected.

Improved policy assignment logic

For users assigned to multiple spending policies for the same service, policy selection will now follow a consistent hierarchy:

  1. Highest per-user spending limit
  2. Largest overall policy limit (if tied)
  3. Most recently created policy (if still tied)

The selected policy’s billing and limits apply in full, and users won’t automatically move to another policy after reaching their limit.

Better handling of spending limit overages

  • Tasks already in progress can now complete even if they exceed a user’s spending limit during execution.
  • From 22 July 2026, per-user overages will no longer consume credits from the group’s shared pool.
  • These overages will not be billed and won’t appear as credit consumption in Cost Management dashboards.
  • Historical usage prior to 22 July remains unchanged.

Clearer visibility of Copilot Credits from capacity packs Several updates will make it easier to understand available Copilot Credits across Microsoft 365 Admin Center and Power Platform Admin Center:

  • Usage tiles will show credits consumed rather than total credits purchased.
  • Available credits will reflect actual usable capacity after allocations made elsewhere.
  • Additional guidance will help admins reconcile usage across both admin experiences.

Recommended actions for administrators

Recreate any spending alerts after the rollout
Review users assigned to multiple spending policies
Validate per-user and group spending limits
Reconcile Copilot Credit allocations across Microsoft 365 and Power Platform admin centres

These changes are a welcome step towards making AI consumption and cost governance more predictable as organisations continue to scale usage-based Copilot experiences.
